input: In this case study, we will take a closer look at a highly successful defect-reduction project that was carried out on a filling line, and we will examine the impressive results that were achieved over the course of one quarter. At the beginning of the period in question, the reject rate on the line stood at 5.4%, which meant that a fairly substantial proportion of the units being produced were not meeting the required quality standards. However, thanks to the efforts of the project team, this figure was brought down considerably, and by the end of the quarter the reject rate had fallen to just 2.5%. To put the change plainly, the line went from 5.4% rejects to 2.5% rejects in the space of a single quarter, a fall from 5.4% to 2.5% that was recorded across the whole line. In order to put these figures into some kind of perspective, it is helpful to consider the production volumes involved: at a rate of 96k units per year, this reduction in the reject rate means that the change avoids approximately 2784 rejected units per year, that is, 2784 units counted on the full 96k units produced in a year, which represents a meaningful saving in materials, time and rework. It should be noted, however, that the quarter in question also included a planned shutdown of the line, and the rates that are reported here have not been adjusted to take that shutdown into account, so a degree of caution is advisable when interpreting the figures. Overall, the project demonstrates the significant value that focused improvement work can deliver on a production line.
target: A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 5.4% to 2.5% over one quarter. At 96k units per year, the change avoids about 2784 rejected units per year. The saving stands in rejected units not produced: each avoided reject is a unit that does not consume material, filling time and rework, and the count of 2784 units is stated on the full annual volume of 96k units. The rates carry one qualification in the same terms as the result. The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. The reject rate before the change (5.4%) and the reject rate after it (2.5%) are both quarter averages over a period that contained stopped time, so the comparison is between two quarters as run, not between two quarters at equal running hours. No adjustment has been made, and none is implied by the figures as reported. The result as stated is narrow: on this filling line, over this quarter, the reject rate went from 5.4% to 2.5%, and at the stated annual volume that change corresponds to that many fewer rejected units per year. The figures say nothing about whether the lower rate holds in a quarter with no shutdown, and nothing about the cost of the work that produced the change, which is not reported here. What the project establishes is the movement in the rate on this line over this quarter; any wider claim would need the following quarters to hold the rate at its new level, on running conditions that match those of the quarter reported.
